# Tomek Link Removal {#sec-imbalenced-tomek}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Tomek Link Removal
:::

Tomek link removal is the practice of identifying Tomek links and removing them from the data set.
A **Tomek Link** is a pair of observations from different classes that have eachother as their nearest neighbor [@tomek1976cnn].
The Tomek link is typically handled by removing the majority observation of the pair instead of removing both observations.

TODO: Diagram

The traditional implementation assumes Euclidean distances,
which in turn assumes you have all numeric predictors and no missing values.

This method is computationally quite fast, as we are only doing one pass of nearest neighbor search.
And that is used to identify observations that could be removed. We aren't doing any sampling.
However, on the other side, we don't have many levers to pull for this method.
It is un uncommon to have few or no points removed when applying Tomek Link removal.

The method also makes the assumption that the noise happens at the border between two classes,
However, that is not true for all data sets.
There is also no notion of importance,
A point deep inside another class may or may not be removed purely based on how close it is to its nearest point.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_tomek()`, which removes Tomek links.

```{r}
#| label: step_tomek
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_tomek(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

This is a good illustration of the point made above about not having many levers to pull.
Only the majority class lost observations, and it lost fewer than a hundred of them out of more than two thousand.
Where the sampling methods let you dial in a target ratio, this method removes the pairs it finds and nothing more.
If those pairs are few, the data set barely changes.

Notice also that `step_tomek()` takes no arguments beyond the outcome and a `seed`.
There is no ratio to set, because the number of observations removed is a property of the data rather than something you choose.

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

{imblearn} provides `TomekLinks()`.

```{python}
#| label: tomeklinks
from imblearn.under_sampling import TomekLinks

X_res, y_res = TomekLinks().fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

The two implementations land within a couple of observations of each other, which is what we should expect given that identifying Tomek links is deterministic once the distance metric is fixed.

By default only the majority class is cleaned.
Setting `sampling_strategy="all"` removes both members of each pair instead, which is the variant mentioned above.

```{python}
#| label: tomeklinks-all
X_res, y_res = TomekLinks(sampling_strategy="all").fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```
